shortDescription: By Luis GarciaArroyo Energy Investment Partners is seeking to raise $900 million for its latest flagship fund to back midsize operators of power-generation and industrial-fuel infrastructure, as the private-equity firm sees opportunity in an overtaxed U.S. electricity grid, according to an investor…

children: Arroyo Energy Investment Partners is seeking to raise $900 million for its latest flagship fund to back midsize operators of power-generation and industrial-fuel infrastructure, as the private-equity firm sees opportunity in an overtaxed U.S. electricity grid, according to an investor presentation viewed by The Wall Street Journal.

The Spring, Texas-based firm has set a goal for Arroyo Investors Fund V above the $680 million it collected for a predecessor pool that wrapped up last year, the presentation showed. Arroyo raised an additional $385 million in co-investment capital for that fund, and the presentation indicates it has deals lined up for the new fund that call for $500 million in co-investments. The firm manages about $4 billion in assets.

Arroyo, sometimes referred to as Arroyo Investors, said in its pitch that a U.S. power grid ill-prepared to cope with rising electricity demand after decades of relatively flat consumption creates unique investment opportunities.

"Electricity consumption is growing for the first time in a generation, and the grid can't keep up," Arroyo said. It cited artificial-intelligence data centers and repatriated manufacturing operations as main demand drivers, in addition to newer vehicles and heating systems that use electricity rather than fossil fuels.

In the presentation, Arroyo sought to differentiate its midmarket, operations-focused strategy from those of generalist buyout firms "without industry expertise" and larger energy-fund general partners that typically write bigger checks. The firm also mentioned "yield-focused midmarket funds" that concentrate on collecting dividends rather than generating returns.
"A gap in the established GP landscape creates compelling opportunities for Arroyo," the firm said.

Arroyo typically invests $100 million to $300 million per deal in operators of energy-infrastructure assets that are often located close to consumers, such as liquefied-natural gas facilities and dedicated power generators, according to the presentation. The firm favors investments in operating or nearly completed projects rather than building from scratch.

Arroyo's past deals included an investment about six years ago in Life Cycle Power, a provider of portable natural gas-fired power generation units for oil-and-gas producers, data centers and utilities, among other users. Arroyo, which had invested $355 million in the Houston company through its third main fund, sold the business late last year to European private-equity peer Partners Group. The deal generated a return multiple before fees of 2.9 times its investment, the presentation showed.

About four years ago, Arroyo also backed Seaside LNG, an operator of liquefaction terminals, storage tanks and fueling vessels mostly in Florida, investing $179 million through its fourth flagship vehicle while co-investors chipped in $149 million. Arroyo, founded in 2003, said its aggregate return across all funds through March came to a net 1.7 times invested capital.

For its new fund, Arroyo has a short-term pipeline of five deals lined up that would total about $875 million from the firm and an additional $100 million from co-investors for each deal, if all of the transactions close as envisioned. Those deals involve assets such as LNG facilities in Texas and Pennsylvania and power installations in Nevada and Florida, according to the presentation, as well as natural gas pipelines across various U.S. states.

Arroyo is raising its new fund as surging electricity demand in the U.S. requires investments not only to build new energy-related projects but also to bulk up mature assets, according to fund managers.

"Old school infrastructure is absolutely associated with this build-out," Brian Callahan, a senior vice president at power-sector investor Brookfield Asset Management, said during a recent industry conference.
As an example, he mentioned natural gas pipelines that ran at roughly half of their capacity last year and that are now targeted for expansion.
"It presents a lot of opportunities for private capital," Callahan said.
